subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 5-month-old girl is evaluated for poor head control and a protruding tongue. Examination shows profound hypotonia, an enlarged tongue, and a hyperactive precordium with a gallop rhythm; the liver edge is also palpable. Chest radiograph shows massive cardiomegaly. Fasting glucose and lactate are normal.
question: Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?
explanation_correct: Pompe disease (type II) results from deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase, also called acid maltase. Glycogen accumulates within lysosomes of cardiac and skeletal muscle and liver, producing cardiomegaly, hypotonia, an enlarged tongue, and early death from heart failure; blood glucose is characteristically normal.

explanation_incorrect.A: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori disease) causes hepatomegaly and mild fasting hypoglycemia with normal lactate, not massive cardiomegaly in infancy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes severe fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly, not isolated cardiomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.C: Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen disease) causes hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, and cirrhosis, not lysosomal glycogen accumulation with cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease) presents in older patients with exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria, not in infancy with cardiomegaly.

educationalObjective: Infantile hypotonia, macroglossia, and massive cardiomegaly indicate Pompe disease, a lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.
